nodes.text: v. emulsion

Kathy drove that baby blue Plymouth voyager minivan with fake wood strip down the side through blasted Utah desert red, summer heat ashimmer undulating black tarmac horizon above and dashboard stickiness below, smelted diet coke tootsie roll together into this pitch tar potpourri.

The black and white border collie sat up front sniffing at trying so hard AC, freon happy doggie grinning out polka-dot tinted childproof glass. Further back were four children between ages eight and eleven, two borrowed, two her own from one marriage still on-going after all these years.
The kids tired of giving long haul truckers the middle-finger, that and alternately pumping their fists to summon the big-rig bellows, a noise that had ceased to startle her a thousand miles ago.
Kathy been driving without stopping for sleeping used to pulling all nighters picking up twelve hour doubles.

She listened to books on tape on loan from the library in these cheap plastic containers that hold dozens, easy to lose track of, mysteries mostly, never so much yawning as the internal tape deck automatically righted itself and the story continued on.
The tapes were weird, could go in one of four ways, upside-down, right-side down, front to back, any which way but loose.

Before the trip she gave the children each a roll of quarters to spend on arcade games and treats from roadside convenience stores along the way. Said, but if you ask when we gonna get there, you gotta give me back a quarter, each, which kept them on each other honest without fail.

She stopped in towns along the way, empty places just off the main drag. All the gas station people looked semi-familial bred-in amongst exhaust fume expanse and quiet nothingness where the roads did not seem to meet.
They were the greasy and deep mistrusting, pock-measured and toothless grinning carnal friendlies, cash only as a courtesy.

In this one place, there was this one guy. Shirt off caked in mud shingled up and down his torso, the joints dry crackling crumbling away a fine pink powder. He stumbled into the gas station, his sculpted hair at angles, he was asking for smokes, lucky strike, precisely.
Kathy had this lecture running in the back of her mind. Formulated working as a respiratory therapist since getting licensed some fifteen odd years ago.

But here in this part of America, where all smoked, all died choking coughing oxygen deficient death, where vultures circled grasping lighters to breasts, flicking alive nubile flame with claw talon spur, to drop from way up above on quarry, smoke em if you got em, the innerstate of mind motto.

Hell, even Kathy smoked when she was sigh so young. All the doctors and staff who trained her made her, all those hospital people sneaking out to be among their own for five or so. True colors fixing for a fix, but she got pregnant and stopped and it was somehow so easy to stand here and judge now.

She held her breath because the air was changing and there was nothing she could do to stop it. More than a minute out here in this mess, the heat taking over her breathing for her, animal gulping almost mouth wide open, hiding it with a folded triptych map with highlighted marker lines marking the way there.

Inside the one room store a desktop fan oscillated shreds of paper, the young woman at the counter getting ready to birth another. The sexless uncertainty inside her felt just as lovely that sweet shared nicotine fix, its hyperrabbit heart amniotic aflitter. Besides breathing for people, Kathy delivered babies, too.

That counter top tending distended boggle-bubble belly always dreaming of discoveries some such other lights and sounds, the sweet warm taste of shared mother fluid all it does know with any real certainty.

The lecture, oh yes, the lecture. Starting and stopping as the mud man reaches into an outdoor ice cooler, grabs cube handfuls washing himself clean rivers of clear revealing almost beautiful skin. Rubbing the ice all over like soap wetting away his pits and back and round and around his belly button.
He wrings out hands over head rubbing remaining sliver cubes into scalp letting them melt but quick in that sudden direct heat from up there that god's eye.
The ice water runs off him into the dust and darkens it and is gone.
The highway off in the near-distance echoing with whirs and booms and the thudding of tires on uneven terrain, straight and certain for-almost-ever.
The kids in the car watched Kathy pump gas she knew it time to move on. Her legs and back protested further interment anticipating the journey more so its completion.

When she was just a kid she worked in Cedar-Sinai, taking care of Ronald Reagan still just Governor of California. She got this dread when word spread him taking a stab at the biggest thing of all because even back then he was already showing signs of senile dementia.

Her best friend Becky told her the Richard Gere story firsthand near two in the morning because Becky was the first person to be lost in all that and Kathy knew she was telling truth. That and she heard the story months before anyone else. Also remembering Arnold Schwarzenegger a near crush from afar.

Him the magnetic center of Venice Beach, her childhood stomp, her mother owning all that beach front property which put her in the mystic proximity of celebrity that defined her youth. The famous always getting sick or getting themselves sick. Their lungs the first to go.
Cancer, emphysema, dark shadow splotches on uncertain x-rays, pneumonia, this in the late seventies early eighties, gay cancer spreading among the bright and beautiful you never would guess.

Kathy's husband in Nova Scotia for six weeks. So she decides to call up Mom, plans to deliver the lazy summer break children to her, drop them off and head up to that undiscovered part of Canada she has never been to herself.
This opportunity to be alone by herself, wants it more than anything all of a sudden desperate. Wants the cold and if not cold, the cool. She can do that go to a whole nother place entire.
The road lays itself out, the creeping middle finger extending, expecting the unforgivable, nodding beckoning damning yes you.
The kids slam the sliding side door open rushing out to pee and pee-pee dance in waiting.

They rummage through nondescript cheap candy in clear plastic bags sealed up top with a thin ribbon of yellow, they flip through magazines they've already seen too much already, they play a quick game of Galaga squirting out needle shots at tiny building-block primary-color-coded insect invader adversaries,

outer space milieu smack dab firm in the wasted west, the layer of dust on everything a fine enough silt changing the way people cough their teeth becoming nubbins worn away to nothing by the grit in everything else eaten drunk, selling dead lizards horny toads with fake engorged enlarged horny parts.
She keeps the children away from the curios as best she can.
